subhead: Take a free practice quiz or get instant, explained answers to Threat Awareness and Reporting Program (TARP) questions — recognize foreign intelligence and terrorism threats without the guesswork.
metaTitle: TARP Training Quiz & Practice Questions | Cambo
metaDescription: Free Threat Awareness and Reporting Program (TARP) quiz and practice questions with instant, explained answers. Elicitation, surveillance, and reporting.
whyItWorks: TARP scenarios ask you to recognize elicitation attempts and suspicious contacts that are deliberately designed to look innocent. Cambo reads the exact scenario on your screen and explains why it is or isn't a reportable indicator, not just the answer.

sampleQuestions.q: What is elicitation, in the context of TARP training?
options: A formal interview conducted by a security officer
A technique used to subtly extract information without the target realizing they are being questioned
A method of encrypting sensitive communications
A background investigation step required for clearance renewal
sampleQuestions.a: A technique used to subtly extract information from someone without them realizing they're being questioned — often through casual conversation rather than direct interrogation.

sampleQuestions.q: You are approached online by someone claiming to be a recruiter who asks detailed questions about your unit's deployment schedule. What should you do?
options: Answer only the questions that are unclassified
Block the account and take no further action
Report the contact to your security officer or counterintelligence point of contact
Ask the recruiter to verify their credentials before responding
sampleQuestions.a: Report the contact to your security officer or counterintelligence point of contact — unsolicited requests for operational details are a classic TARP reporting indicator.

sampleQuestions.q: A stranger at a conference offers to pay for your travel and accommodations in exchange for a private "consulting" conversation about your work. What TARP concern does this raise?
options: It is a routine networking opportunity with no security implications
It is an ethics violation but not a counterintelligence concern
It is acceptable as long as you avoid discussing classified information
It is a potential elicitation and recruitment attempt — unsolicited financial incentives tied to work information are a classic red flag
sampleQuestions.a: It's a potential elicitation and recruitment attempt — unsolicited financial incentives tied to sharing work-related information are a classic red flag covered in TARP training.

sampleQuestions.q: What is the difference between elicitation and a direct interrogation?
options: Elicitation is subtle and disguised as normal conversation, while interrogation is direct, recognizable questioning
Elicitation is lawful, while interrogation is always unlawful
Elicitation happens online, while interrogation happens in person
There is no practical difference between the two
sampleQuestions.a: Elicitation is subtle and often disguised as normal conversation, designed so the target doesn't realize information is being extracted, while interrogation is direct, recognizable questioning.

sampleQuestions.q: Why does TARP training emphasize reporting suspicious contacts even if you're not sure they're a real threat?
options: Because failing to report any contact is itself a punishable offense
Because counterintelligence analysts can connect a single contact to patterns across other reports
Because every reported contact triggers an immediate investigation
Because reporting transfers legal liability away from the individual
sampleQuestions.a: Because counterintelligence professionals are better positioned to assess a pattern across multiple reports — a single contact might seem minor, but reporting lets analysts connect it to other information.

sampleQuestions.q: Which of the following is a common TARP indicator involving social media?
options: A former colleague requesting to connect after leaving the service
An official unit account posting a public affairs release
An unfamiliar profile that quickly becomes overly friendly and asks pointed questions about your job, clearance, or deployment
A recruiter advertising civilian job openings to veterans
sampleQuestions.a: An unfamiliar profile that quickly becomes overly friendly and starts asking pointed questions about your job, clearance, or deployment — a common vector for elicitation online.

faqs.q: How often is TARP training required?
faqs.a: Annually for Army personnel and DoD civilians, per Army Regulation 381-12, with similar requirements across other service branches.

faqs.q: Who has to complete TARP training?
faqs.a: All Army personnel, DoD civilians, and contractors — the requirement is most explicitly codified in the Army but applies broadly across DoD counterintelligence awareness programs.

faqs.q: What's the difference between TARP and Insider Threat training?
faqs.a: TARP focuses specifically on recognizing and reporting foreign intelligence entity contacts and elicitation attempts. Insider Threat training covers the broader range of risks from trusted insiders, including non-espionage-related risks.

faqs.q: Is Cambo affiliated with the DoD or Army?
faqs.a: No. Cambo is an independent study tool, not produced or endorsed by the Department of Defense or U.S. Army.

faqs.q: What are reportable contacts under TARP?
faqs.a: Unsolicited contact from foreign nationals seeking sensitive information, suspicious requests over social media, and any attempt to recruit or elicit information through relationships or financial incentives.

faqs.q: Where do I report a suspicious contact?
faqs.a: Through your command's counterintelligence office or security officer — reporting channels are covered specifically in the training.
